cards.title: Retrieve before checking
cards.prompt: You reread a page and it feels familiar. Design one short next step that would give you better evidence about what you can explain tomorrow. Say what you would compare after checking.
cards.model: Close the page, explain its central idea from memory, and keep that first explanation. Check against the source and name one missing relationship or error. cards.title: Match the claim to the evidence
cards.prompt: A fictional study finds that learners who use a new study tool have higher scores. They chose whether to use it. Explain why the result alone does not establish that the tool caused the difference. Name one useful design improvement.
cards.model: Self-selection permits other differences, such as prior preparation or available time, to contribute to the score difference. Random assignment with a defined comparison can improve causal interpretation, while still requiring attention to adherence, measurement and the study population. A held-out prediction test answers a different question from a causal study.
cards.compare: Identify the alternative explanation you named and whether your design change addresses it. Keep prediction and causal effects separate.

cards.title: Separate ventilation, exchange and delivery
cards.prompt: A classmate says: “The diaphragm moved, so oxygen delivery must be adequate.” Explain two missing links in that reasoning without diagnosing a patient.
cards.model: Diaphragm movement contributes to ventilation through changes in thoracic volume and pressure. Gas exchange and transport still depend on other conditions. Oxygen delivery depends on blood flow and oxygen content, including hemoglobin, so neither visible movement nor saturation alone establishes adequate delivery.
cards.compare: Check that you named ventilation and at least two later requirements. Remove any conclusion about a real patient that these observations cannot support.

cards.title: Keep measurement, units and time together
cards.prompt: A fictional uniformly sampled signal uses 250 samples per second. A feature is 50 sample intervals after a marked start. Give the elapsed time and explain what would be missing if you only reported “50.”

The number 50 alone does not state whether it means a sample index, intervals or seconds; voltage amplitude would need its own units. This arithmetic does not identify the biological source or diagnose a pattern.

cards.title: Interpret evidence in context
cards.prompt: A fictional report says a result was above the laboratory threshold. A peer concludes the suspected condition is proven. Name the missing information needed to assess that claim; do not choose a treatment or a numerical clinical cutoff.
cards.model: The analyte, assay, units, intended threshold, clinical question and prior probability matter. Other processes may produce an elevated result, and the testing pathway determines its role. “Above threshold” is an observation, not by itself proof of one condition. The amount of uncertainty cannot be inferred from that phrase alone.

cards.title: Separate a buffer from a physiological response
cards.prompt: A learner treats chemical buffering and a change in ventilation as the same process because both can affect pH. Distinguish the mechanisms and explain why a compensation rule needs an appropriate clinical context.
cards.model: Chemical buffering involves reversible acid-base reactions. A change in ventilation changes carbon dioxide elimination, while renal processes affect acid excretion and bicarbonate handling. These mechanisms differ in what changes and on what time scale. An expected compensation is a context-dependent check; a match does not explain every cause or exclude every additional process.
cards.compare: Check the mechanism you assigned to each process and the limit you placed on the compensation check.
